title: Reward-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
claim: Adding our reward-conditioning to strong baselines improves performance across single-task, multi-task, vision, and steerability settings.
layout: 4 panels in a row, each with paired horizontal bars, baseline vs ours
description: A single horizontal strip of four small bar-chart panels. Each panel has a title and a task count: Single-Task (23 tasks), Multi-Task (33 tasks), Vision-Based (9 tasks), and Policy Steerability (28 tasks). Each panel has two horizontal bars with error bars. The top bar is blue and shows the baseline (SimbaV2, BRC, DrQV2, SimbaV2). The bottom bar is green and shows the same baseline plus RCRL. Labels sit inside the bars in white text. Light dashed gridlines and a numeric x-axis run along the bottom of each panel. In every panel the green bar is longer than the blue one. The gap is largest in the steerability panel, where the score goes from about 0.27 to about 0.58. The eye goes first to the green bars.
caption: Results summary. RCRL improves the performance of strong baselines in both single and multi-task settings (Figure [ref]). As a secondary capability, RCRL increases the steerability of the trained policy without further training (Figure [ref]).
abstract: Sample-efficient reinforcement learning typically uses a fixed reward function both to guide exploration and to supervise learning. However, the same experience can provide supervision under multiple related reward specifications, even when the objective of interest remains fixed. We introduce Reward-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning (RCRL), an off-policy approach that collects experience under a nominal objective while training a reward-conditioned agent using counterfactual rewards recomputed from replay. RCRL constructs alternative reward specifications by perturbing the nominal reward, providing diverse supervision without additional environment interaction. Across single-task, multi-task, and vision-based control benchmarks, RCRL improves nominal task performance and sample efficiency when integrated with strong RL backbones. As a secondary capability, the learned policies support zero-shot behavioral adjustment toward related objectives without further training. These results demonstrate that diverse reward supervision can improve learning of a predefined objective while also enabling policy steerability.
